newsitem.title: GERMANY: New blows fly in German tax battle.
newsitem.headline: New blows fly in German tax battle.

text.p: German politicians seized on the introduction of a government tax bill into parliament on Friday to crank up the volume in a war of words which broke out after the collapse of cross-party tax talks this week.

In a debate on Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1999 bill to complete 30 billion marks ($17.5 billion) in tax cuts, coalition and opposition leaders blamed each other for barring action to put Germany's 4.5 million unemployed back to work.

"You want to block and brake," Waigel accused the opposition Social Democrats (SPD). "That means uncertainty for investors and consumers. Uncertainty delays recovery and weakens growth. And unemployment stays."
Looking to next year's general election, he added: "You want to use this alarming scenario as campaign ammunition."

Talks between Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition and the SPD on seeking an early compromise on tax reforms broke up on Wednesday in acrimony. After blasting each other in the media, recriminations continued in the Bundestag lower house.

Repeating accusations Waigel's plans to cut taxes would rip a hole of over 50 billion marks in state finances, SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss said: "For any of Waigel's predecessors that would have been reason enough to resign."

The start of parliamentary proceedings on the tax reforms is likely to dampen the hopes of even the most ardent optimist that the government can convince the SPD-controlled Bundesrat upper house to back its income and corporate tax cuts.
But Kohl still said a compromise could be reached on the main tax reforms in parliament's conflict-resolution process.
"You can expect we will reach an agreement in the upper house in the autumn," Kohl told industrialists in Duesseldorf.

Outside parliament, a potential SPD challenger to Kohl in the October 1998 general election, accused Waigel of wanting to raise, not cut, taxes this year in order to qualify for European monetary union (EMU).
Lower Saxony premier Gerhard Schroeder told the n-tv news channel in an interview to be aired on Saturday that such a tax hike would be a "fatal mistake for the new currency".

Waigel has not ruled out a spending freeze, tax hikes or a cut in welfare benefits to cut the budget deficit below the Maastricht treaty limit of three percent of GDP this year to ensure Germany joins the EMU starting lineup in 1999.

SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine also opted out of the Bundestag tax debate, instead announcing in a newspaper interview that he would also pull the plug on consensus talks on pensions reform with Kohl in the wake of the collapse of the tax talks.
Lafontaine told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung his party had reached the "fine-tuning" stage of drafting its own long-awaited comprehensive tax programme.

He said the SPD's tax model would foresee an income tax model cutting the bottom rate to 22.5 percent but keeping today's top rate of 53 percent. Waigel's tax reform proposes income taxes running from 15 to 39 percent.

The stand-off between government and opposition was also on full show in the Bundesrat on Friday, where the SPD again voted down a bill to abolish a capital trading tax on businesses -- a measure held up in parliament for over two years. ($ = 1.714 German Marks)
